This strongly favors chronic inflammatory arthropathies over acute episodic conditions. Rheumatoid arthritis is the most likely given its classic symmetric, erosive, small-joint-predominant onset (wrists early), with frequent knee involvement and decade-long progression; seropositivity and radiographic changes would support this. Osteoarthritis is plausible but less likely to prominently involve wrists (typically sparing them except in erosive or post-traumatic cases) and usually shows more asymmetry and load-related patterns; however, generalized OA or nodal OA can present bilaterally and chronically. Psoriatic arthritis fits well—can be symmetric, involve wrists/knees, and persist for years; dactylitis, nail pitting, or psoriasis history would increase confidence. SLE is included due to symmetric inflammatory arthralgia/arthritis (often non-erosive), multi-year course, and frequent wrist/knee involvement—but systemic features (rash, renal, hematologic) are absent from current data. Chronic gout is lower-confidence: while long-standing gout can become polyarticular and chronic, the absence of reported acute flares (and negative response to the gout-trigger question—though not definitive) makes classic recurrent gout less likely; however, chronic tophaceous gout can mimic RA clinically and should not be excluded without serum urate or imaging."}
